title: Electrolysis
tagline: Understand ionic conduction, electrode reactions and applications of electrolysis.

overview.intro: Electrolysis is the chemical decomposition of an electrolyte in molten state or aqueous solution by the passage of direct electric current. It involves movement of ions to oppositely charged electrodes and their discharge through oxidation and reduction reactions. This chapter examines electrolytes and non-electrolytes, terms such as anode, cathode and ionisation, electrolysis of selected substances, and applications including electroplating and refining.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: Chemical change caused by electric current in electrolyte

facts.label: Applications
facts.value: Electroplating, electrorefining, extraction, electrolysis of compounds

learningOutcomes: Define electrolyte, electrolysis, electrodes and related terms.
Explain ion migration and electrode reactions during electrolysis.
Describe electrolysis of molten lead bromide, acidified water and copper(II) sulphate solution.
Compare outcomes with inert and active electrodes where applicable.
Explain principles and uses of electroplating and electrorefining.

blocks.text: Electrolytes are compounds that conduct electricity in molten state or aqueous solution due to the presence of mobile ions and undergo chemical decomposition. Strong electrolytes ionise or dissociate completely, while weak electrolytes do so partially. Non-electrolytes do not produce ions in solution and therefore do not conduct electricity in that form.

In an electrolytic cell, the anode is the electrode connected to the positive terminal of the battery and attracts anions, while the cathode is connected to the negative terminal and attracts cations. Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode. The direction of conventional current in the external circuit is opposite to electron flow.

items: Metallic conduction involves electrons; electrolytic conduction involves ions.
Electrolysis requires a direct current (DC) source.
Ions are discharged at electrodes, forming new substances.
Concentration, nature of electrodes and position in electrochemical series influence products.

blocks.text: Molten lead bromide (PbBr2) contains mobile Pb2+ and Br− ions. When direct current is passed through it using inert electrodes, Pb2+ ions migrate to the cathode where they gain electrons and are reduced to molten lead. Br− ions migrate to the anode where they lose electrons and are oxidised to bromine vapour.

This example clearly shows decomposition of a binary molten electrolyte into its constituent elements. No water is present, so competing reactions from water do not occur. The overall reaction is PbBr2(l) → Pb(l) + Br2(g).

items.note: Reduction: gain of electrons by lead ions.
Oxidation: loss of electrons by bromide ions.

learn.title: Electrolysis of Acidified Water and Copper(II) Sulphate

blocks.text: Acidified water (dilute sulphuric acid) conducts electricity and decomposes to give hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode in a 2:1 volume ratio. Water molecules provide H+ and OH− ions for discharge; sulphate ions generally remain in solution with inert electrodes. The process demonstrates decomposition of water.

Electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulphate depends on electrode material. With inert electrodes (platinum/carbon), copper is deposited at the cathode and oxygen is evolved at the anode, while the solution becomes acidic. With copper electrodes, copper dissolves from the anode and is deposited at the cathode, keeping the concentration of Cu2+ in solution nearly constant.

blocks.caption: Copper(II) sulphate electrolysis outcomes
rows: Copper dissolves from anode; Cu2+ concentration maintained

blocks.text: Electroplating is the process of depositing a thin layer of a desired metal on an object using electrolysis. The article to be plated is made the cathode, a plate or rod of the plating metal is made the anode, and a soluble salt solution of the plating metal is used as electrolyte. Conditions such as current, temperature and concentration are controlled for a smooth deposit.

Electrorefining purifies metals by making the impure metal the anode and a pure strip the cathode in a suitable electrolyte. The pure metal dissolves from the anode and deposits on the cathode, while impurities either fall as anode mud or remain in solution. Copper refining is an important industrial example.

items.meaning: Depositing a coating of one metal on another object by electrolysis.
Purifying a metal using electrolysis with impure metal as anode.
Insoluble impurities that collect below the anode during electrorefining.

learn.title: Factors Affecting Products and Practical Applications

blocks.text: The products of electrolysis of aqueous solutions depend on the relative ease of discharge of ions, concentration of ions and nature of electrodes. For example, at the cathode, ions lower in the reactivity/electrochemical tendency may be discharged preferentially, while active anodes can participate in the reaction instead of releasing anions.

Applications of electrolysis include extraction of reactive metals, manufacture of chemicals, electroplating for protection and appearance, and electrorefining for purity. Understanding electrode reactions allows prediction of mass changes, gas evolution and changes in electrolyte composition.

items: Use clean surfaces for uniform electroplating.
Low, steady current often gives better plating quality.
In electrorefining, anode loses mass while cathode gains mass.
Identify oxidation at anode and reduction at cathode in all examples.

keyPoints: Electrolysis decomposes electrolytes using direct current through mobile ions.
Cations move to the cathode and are reduced; anions move to the anode and are oxidised.
Molten lead bromide yields lead at cathode and bromine at anode.
Acidified water produces hydrogen and oxygen in 2:1 volume ratio with inert electrodes.
Products of CuSO4 electrolysis depend on whether electrodes are inert or copper.
In electroplating, the object is the cathode and the plating metal is the anode.
Electrorefining transfers pure metal from impure anode to pure cathode.
Nature of electrodes, ion concentration and discharge tendency affect products.
Electrolytic conduction is due to ions, unlike metallic conduction by electrons.
Balanced electrode equations clarify oxidation and reduction processes.

vocabulary.meaning: Chemical decomposition of an electrolyte by passage of electric current.
A substance that conducts electricity in molten or aqueous state by ions and decomposes.
The positive electrode in an electrolytic cell where oxidation occurs.
The negative electrode in an electrolytic cell where reduction occurs.
A positively charged ion that moves toward the cathode.
A negatively charged ion that moves toward the anode.
Loss of electrons at the anode during electrolysis.
Gain of electrons at the cathode during electrolysis.
Coating an object with a metal layer using electrolysis.
Purification of a metal by electrolytic transfer from anode to cathode.
An electrode that does not take part chemically in electrolysis, such as platinum or graphite.
Insoluble impurities deposited below the anode during refining.

questions.prompt: During electrolysis, reduction occurs at the:
questions.answer: cathode
questions.explanation: Cations gain electrons at the cathode, which is a reduction process.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse anode (oxidation) with cathode (reduction).

questions.prompt: In the electrolysis of molten lead bromide, the product at the cathode is:
questions.answer: lead
questions.explanation: Pb2+ ions are reduced at the cathode to form molten lead.
questions.commonMistake: Bromine is formed at the anode, not at the cathode.

questions.prompt: Which statement about electrolytic conduction is correct?
options: It is due to flow of electrons in solution
It is due to movement of ions
It does not cause chemical change
questions.answer: It is due to movement of ions
questions.explanation: Electrolytes conduct electricity through mobile ions that are discharged at electrodes.
questions.commonMistake: Electron flow occurs in metals; ions carry charge in electrolytes.

questions.prompt: During electrolysis of acidified water with inert electrodes, gases are produced in the ratio:
questions.answer: 2:1 hydrogen to oxygen
questions.explanation: Water decomposes to give two volumes of hydrogen for every one volume of oxygen.
questions.commonMistake: Hydrogen is produced at the cathode in greater volume.

questions.prompt: In electroplating an iron spoon with silver, the spoon is made the:
questions.answer: cathode
questions.explanation: The object to be plated is the cathode so that metal ions are reduced and deposited on it.
questions.commonMistake: The plating metal is usually the anode, not the object.

questions.prompt: Oxidation involves:
questions.answer: loss of electrons
questions.explanation: At the anode, species lose electrons during electrolysis, which is oxidation.
questions.commonMistake: Reduction is gain of electrons; oxidation is loss.

questions.prompt: In electrolysis of aqueous CuSO4 using copper electrodes, the anode:
questions.answer: dissolves
questions.explanation: With active copper electrodes, copper atoms at the anode lose electrons and enter solution as Cu2+ ions.
questions.commonMistake: Active electrodes can participate; oxygen evolution occurs with inert electrodes.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly matches electrode and process in electrolysis?
questions.answer: Anode – oxidation
questions.explanation: Anions are discharged by losing electrons at the anode, so oxidation occurs there.
questions.commonMistake: Remember: anode oxidation, cathode reduction.

questions.prompt: The negative electrode in an electrolytic cell is called the ________.
questions.answer: cathode
questions.explanation: The cathode is connected to the negative terminal and attracts cations.
questions.commonMistake: The anode is the positive electrode in electrolysis.

questions.prompt: In electrorefining of copper, impurities collect below the anode as ________.
questions.answer: anode mud
questions.explanation: Insoluble impurities fall off the impure anode and form anode mud.
questions.commonMistake: Soluble impurities may remain in the electrolyte instead.

questions.prompt: A substance that does not conduct electricity in solution because it does not form ions is a ________.
questions.answer: non-electrolyte
questions.explanation: Non-electrolytes do not dissociate into ions and hence do not undergo electrolysis.
questions.commonMistake: Weak electrolytes conduct partially; non-electrolytes do not ionise.

questions.prompt: Define electrolysis.
questions.answer: Electrolysis is the chemical decomposition of an electrolyte in molten state or aqueous solution by the passage of direct electric current.
questions.explanation: The definition includes decomposition, electrolyte state and use of electric current.
questions.commonMistake: Mention that a chemical change occurs, not just conduction.

questions.prompt: Write the electrode reactions for electrolysis of molten lead bromide.
questions.answer: At cathode: Pb2+ + 2e− → Pb. At anode: 2Br− → Br2 + 2e−.
questions.explanation: Lead ions are reduced and bromide ions are oxidised at respective electrodes.
questions.commonMistake: Balance electrons lost and gained in the half-reactions.

questions.prompt: State the products at cathode and anode during electrolysis of acidified water using inert electrodes.
questions.answer: Hydrogen gas is liberated at the cathode and oxygen gas is liberated at the anode. The gases are produced in the volume ratio 2:1 (hydrogen:oxygen).
questions.explanation: Discharge of ions from water leads to decomposition into its constituent gases.
questions.commonMistake: Identify the correct gas at each electrode.

questions.prompt: Why is the article to be electroplated made the cathode?
questions.answer: The article is made the cathode because metal ions in the electrolyte are positively charged and migrate to the cathode. There they gain electrons and are deposited as a thin metal coating on the article.
questions.explanation: Reduction of metal ions at the cathode produces the desired plating.
questions.commonMistake: If the article were the anode, it could dissolve instead of being plated.

questions.prompt: Describe the electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulphate using inert electrodes, including observations and electrode reactions.
questions.answer: Using inert electrodes, Cu2+ ions migrate to the cathode and are reduced to copper metal, forming a reddish deposit: Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu. At the anode, hydroxide ions from water are preferentially discharged to produce oxygen gas: 4OH− → 2H2O + O2 + 4e− (overall representation). The blue colour of the solution fades as Cu2+ ions are removed and the solution becomes acidic due to formation of sulphuric acid.
questions.explanation: Electrode choice determines which species are discharged and how the electrolyte changes.
questions.commonMistake: With inert electrodes, copper dissolves from the anode does not occur.

questions.prompt: Explain electrorefining of copper with a labelled description of electrodes, electrolyte and reactions.
questions.answer: In copper electrorefining, a thick block of impure copper is made the anode and a thin sheet of pure copper is made the cathode. The electrolyte is acidified copper(II) sulphate solution. On passing current, copper atoms at the anode lose electrons and go into solution as Cu2+ ions (Cu → Cu2+ + 2e−). At the cathode, Cu2+ ions gain electrons and deposit as pure copper (Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu). Insoluble impurities settle as anode mud while soluble impurities remain in solution.
questions.explanation: Selective transfer of copper results in purification at the cathode.
questions.commonMistake: Clearly identify which electrode is impure and which is pure.

questions.prompt: Compare electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulphate using (i) inert electrodes and (ii) copper electrodes, stating products and changes in electrolyte.
questions.answer: (i) With inert electrodes, copper is deposited at the cathode and oxygen is released at the anode. Cu2+ ions are consumed, so the blue colour fades and the solution becomes acidic. (ii) With copper electrodes, copper is deposited at the cathode while copper dissolves from the anode at an equal rate. The concentration of Cu2+ ions and the blue colour of the solution remain nearly unchanged. In both cases reduction occurs at cathode and oxidation at anode, but the anode reaction differs due to electrode material.
questions.explanation: Active copper anode participates in the reaction, unlike inert electrodes.
questions.commonMistake: State the change (or no change) in electrolyte colour/concentration for each case.

questions.prompt: During electrolysis of molten PbBr2, reddish-brown vapours are seen at one electrode. Identify the electrode and explain the reaction.
questions.answer: Reddish-brown bromine vapours are seen at the anode (positive electrode). Bromide ions migrate to the anode and lose electrons: 2Br− → Br2 + 2e−. This oxidation produces bromine gas/vapour, which appears reddish-brown.
questions.explanation: Anions are discharged at the anode, forming the non-metal element in this case.
questions.commonMistake: Lead is formed at the cathode as a metal, not as vapour.

questions.prompt: A student wants a uniform nickel coating on a key. Suggest suitable anode, cathode and electrolyte, and explain your choices.
questions.answer: Make the key the cathode so nickel deposits on it, use a pure nickel plate as the anode to replenish nickel ions, and use a solution of a soluble nickel salt (such as nickel sulphate) as the electrolyte. On passing current, Ni2+ ions are reduced at the cathode to coat the key, while nickel dissolves from the anode to maintain electrolyte concentration, giving a uniform deposit.
questions.explanation: Correct electrode assignment and electrolyte composition are essential for effective electroplating.
questions.commonMistake: Do not make the object the anode; it must receive the metal deposit.

questions.prompt: Predict and explain the change in mass of cathode and anode during electrorefining of impure copper over time.
questions.answer: The cathode (pure copper sheet) gains mass because Cu2+ ions from the electrolyte are reduced and deposited as pure copper on it. The anode (impure copper block) loses mass because copper atoms are oxidised to Cu2+ ions and pass into solution. The gain in cathode mass is approximately equal to the loss of pure copper from the anode, while insoluble impurities fall as anode mud.
questions.explanation: Mass transfer occurs through dissolution at anode and deposition at cathode.
questions.commonMistake: Account for impurities; not all anode mass becomes cathode deposit.

questions.prompt: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does?
questions.answer: In solid sodium chloride, ions are fixed in a rigid crystal lattice and cannot move, so there are no mobile charge carriers. When molten, the lattice breaks and Na+ and Cl− ions become free to move. These mobile ions carry electric charge through the melt, allowing conduction and electrolysis.
questions.explanation: Electrical conduction in ionic substances requires mobility of ions.
questions.commonMistake: Molten ionic compounds conduct by ions, not by free electrons like metals.
